html:
A Korean Air Lines Boeing 747 flying from New York via Anchorage to Seoul was shot down by a Soviet fighter near Sakhalin on 1 September 1983. All 269 people aboard died, including US congressman Larry McDonald.

The plane had drifted hundreds of kilometres off its route and flew over the Kamchatka Peninsula and then Sakhalin, both sensitive Soviet military areas. A Soviet Su-15 pilot fired missiles on the order of air defence commanders, who took it for a US spy plane. The Soviet Union first denied it, then said the plane had been spying.

The shootdown came at a tense point in the Cold War. Reagan called it a crime against humanity, and the incident hardened opinion against Moscow. The US soon opened its GPS satellite navigation to civilian use.

The cause was long debated. After the USSR gave up the flight recorders in 1992, an international inquiry concluded that the crew had probably left the autopilot on a magnetic heading instead of the inertial navigation system, so the plane drifted. The crew never noticed. Korean Air was the airline.
sum: A Korean Air Lines Boeing 747 flying from New York via Anchorage to Seoul was shot down by a Soviet fighter near Sakhalin on 1 September 1983. All 269 people aboard died, including US congressman Larry McDonald.
